04
Product research · Zoom in
Product research happens in stages
Collect and analyze information about customer needs, market trends, and competitor offerings to decide what to build.
1
Before launch
Study the industry and competitors, and test your concept.
2
Evaluation & feedback
Let customers try it through trials or focus groups.
3
Soft launch
Release to a small group first, then adjust.
4
After launch
Survey customers and keep improving.

06
FOUNDER TRAP
“The pet industry is huge, so my dog-walking app will work.”
A big market proves people spend money. It doesn’t prove anyone wants your product. Pair market data with product evidence, like survey results or prototype feedback.
MKT · MARKET QUESTION
“How many Pinecrest dog owners already pay for dog walking?”
PRD · PRODUCT QUESTION
“Would owners book walks in my app instead of texting a walker?”
Source: https://www.scoutforpets.com/

07
Types of sources
Primary vs. secondary research
YOU COLLECT IT
Primary research
Image created with Gemini.
Who: You or your team gather firsthand data
Cost: Takes more money and time
Fit: Specific to your exact questions
How: Surveys, interviews, focus groups
VS
ALREADY EXISTS
Secondary research
Image created with Gemini.
Who: Uses research others already did
Cost: Cheap, or even free
Fit: Covers general questions
How: Reports, statistics, existing data
Tip: Try conducting your own primary research during product research.

10
Company research
Researching public companies
Public companies are easier to research than private companies.
EASIER TO RESEARCH
Public
Sells shares to the public
Regulators require reports
Shares reports under “Investor Relations”
HARDER TO RESEARCH
Private
Owned privately
Not required to publish reports
Less information available
Look up the parent
Frito-Lay North America is a subsidiary branch, but it belongs to PepsiCo, a public company. Research the parent company too.
Public vs. private companies ↗ · Example: Starbucks Investor Relations ↗

Business databases · 1 of 3
Statista: what’s inside?
TRY IT · SEARCH WITH A QUESTION
Type a full question, like this snack chip search. 
Market Insights
Data from industry reports, with conclusions drawn from the data.
Industry overviews
Look under “Statistics” for data-driven summaries of an industry.
Company statistics & facts
Combined data and statistics about specific companies.
Statista summarizes reports. It is NOT the actual industry report or annual report.
GULLIVER PREP · ENTREPRENEURSHIP RESEARCH
15
Business databases · 2 of 3
Gale Business: Insights
Industry overviews
Search by industry code or name for overviews, competitors, and market share.
★ BEST FOR COMPETITORS
Competitor analysis
Company profiles with overviews and financial statements.
Trade & academic journals
Articles on every business topic. Scroll down an industry page to find them.
Profiles summarize. They are NOT the actual industry report or annual report.
ACCESS: MYLIBRARY › A-Z DATABASES ↗
16
Business databases · 3 of 3
Nexis Uni: what’s inside?
WHAT YOU’LL FIND
Market insights: data from industry reports
Company research: reports, including some SWOTs
Product research: patents and product articles
Bonus: lots of legal documents
HOW TO SEARCH
Find a company
Type the company name, then choose “Companies.”
Find an industry
Select “Market Insight” in the top bar, then filter.
Find a publication
Search for a specific newspaper or journal by name.
Reports summarize. They are NOT the actual industry report or annual report.

18
AI and research · Try it
Try these Gemini prompts
OPTION 1 · KEYWORD BUILDER
Learn the industry’s language
I’m a high school student writing a business plan for [your idea]. List 10 keywords to search business databases, explain 3 key terms simply, and name my industry so I can find its NAICS code. Do not give me statistics.
Use it to: get search terms for Gale, Statista, and Nexis Uni.
OPTION 2 · RESEARCH PLANNER
Plan what to investigate
I’m a high school student researching the market for [your idea]. Suggest 5 research questions about customers, competitors, and trends. Name competitors to look up, and match each question to a source type. Mark anything you’re unsure about.
Use it to: know what to look up, then verify every lead.
1
Fill in [your idea]
2
Verify in the 3 databases
3
Cite the database, not Gemini
